name: Daniel

overview.author: Daniel, a Judean taken to Babylon as a youth, who served in the courts of Babylon and Persia (7:1; 9:2; 12:4; Matthew 24:15).
overview.date: Events from 605 BC (the first deportation) to about 536 BC (the third year of Cyrus), written in the 6th century BC.
overview.audience: Jewish exiles in Babylon and God’s people living under hostile world powers in every age.
overview.setting: Babylon and Persia, in the courts of Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, Darius the Mede, and Cyrus.
overview.purpose: To show that the God of Israel is sovereign over all kingdoms, to encourage faithfulness under pressure, and to reveal that God’s everlasting kingdom will triumph through the Son of Man.
overview.structure: Stories of Daniel and his friends in the foreign court (1–6) and Daniel’s apocalyptic visions of world kingdoms and God’s final kingdom (7–12). Chapters 2:4b-7:28 are written in Aramaic.

outline.title: Daniel and His Friends in Babylon

items.title: Four beasts and the Son of Man
Daniel’s prayer and the seventy weeks

themes.title: God’s Sovereignty Over Nations
themes.text: “The Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will” (4:17).

themes.title: Faithfulness in a Foreign Culture
themes.text: Daniel and his friends serve well while refusing to compromise.

themes.title: God’s Deliverance
themes.text: God rescues from the furnace and the lions, and even when He doesn’t, His people stay faithful (3:18).

themes.title: Pride and Humility
themes.text: Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar learn that God humbles the proud.

themes.title: Prayer
themes.text: Daniel prays regularly, boldly, and with confession.

themes.title: The Coming Kingdom
themes.text: God’s kingdom, like a stone not cut by human hands, will fill the earth.

themes.title: The Son of Man
themes.text: One like a son of man receives an everlasting dominion (7:13–14).

themes.title: Resurrection
themes.text: Daniel 12:2 clearly teaches the resurrection of the dead.

christInBook.text: Jesus’ favorite title, “Son of Man,” comes from this vision; He claimed it at His trial (Mark 14:62).
The stone cut without hands is Christ’s kingdom crushing earthly empires.
A fourth figure in the fire pictures God’s presence with His people in suffering.
An anointed one is “cut off” after the appointed weeks, pointing to the Messiah’s death.
Resurrection to everlasting life fulfilled through Christ (John 5:28–29).

crossReferences.note: Shutting lions’ mouths and quenching fire.

reflection: Daniel “resolved” not to defile himself (1:8). Where do you need to settle your convictions before pressure comes?
How does 3:17–18 shape your faith when God might not deliver in the way you hope?
What does Nebuchadnezzar’s story teach you about pride?
Daniel prayed three times a day even when it was illegal. What does your prayer life look like under pressure?
How does the vision of the Son of Man receiving an eternal kingdom give you hope today?

chapterList.title: Daniel’s Resolve
chapterList.summary: Nebuchadnezzar takes young nobles from Judah, including Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, to train in Babylon and renames them. Daniel resolves not to defile himself with the king’s food and proposes a ten-day test of vegetables and water. God gives them favor, knowledge, and wisdom ten times better than all the magicians.
questions: Why might Daniel have refused the king’s food?
How did Daniel show wisdom and respect in his request (1:8–14)?
Who gave the young men their success (1:9, 17)?

chapterList.title: The Dream of the Great Statue
chapterList.summary: Nebuchadnezzar demands his wise men tell him his dream and its meaning. Daniel and his friends pray, and God reveals the mystery. Daniel blesses God, who “changes times and seasons.” The statue of gold, silver, bronze, iron, and clay represents successive kingdoms, struck by a stone cut without hands that becomes a mountain filling the earth: God’s eternal kingdom.
questions: How did Daniel respond to the crisis (2:17–18)?
What does Daniel’s prayer reveal about God (2:20–23)?
What does the stone represent, and how is it fulfilled in Christ?

chapterList.title: The Fiery Furnace
chapterList.summary: Nebuchadnezzar sets up a golden image and commands all to worship it. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refuse: “Our God... is able to deliver us... But if not... we will not serve your gods.” They are thrown into the furnace, but a fourth figure walks with them, and they come out unharmed, not even smelling of smoke.
questions: What makes the friends’ answer in 3:16–18 so powerful?
Who is the fourth man in the fire (3:25)?
How does God meet His people in their trials (Isaiah 43:2)?

chapterList.title: Nebuchadnezzar Humbled
chapterList.summary: Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a great tree cut down. Daniel interprets: the king will lose his sanity and live like an animal until he acknowledges that the Most High rules. A year later, boasting over Babylon, he is struck. When his reason returns, he praises God: “Those who walk in pride he is able to humble.”
questions: What did Daniel counsel the king to do (4:27)?
What sin brought judgment (4:30)?
How does the king’s testimony (4:34–37) show a changed heart?

chapterList.title: The Writing on the Wall
chapterList.summary: At a feast, King Belshazzar drinks from the temple vessels and praises idols. A hand writes on the wall. Daniel interprets: “Mene, Mene, Tekel, and Parsin.” God has numbered the kingdom; Belshazzar is weighed and found wanting. That night he is killed, and Darius the Mede takes the kingdom.
questions: Why was Belshazzar’s sin worse in light of what he knew (5:22)?
What does “weighed in the balances and found wanting” mean?
How should we treat what is holy?

chapterList.title: Daniel in the Lions’ Den
chapterList.summary: Officials, jealous of Daniel, trick Darius into banning prayer to anyone but the king for thirty days. Daniel keeps praying three times a day toward Jerusalem. He is thrown to the lions, but God shuts their mouths. Darius decrees that all should fear Daniel’s God, “for he is the living God.”
questions: What could the officials find against Daniel (6:4–5)?
What did Daniel do when he heard the decree (6:10)?
How does Darius’s decree (6:26–27) magnify God?

chapterList.title: Four Beasts and the Son of Man
chapterList.summary: Daniel sees four great beasts rise from the sea, representing kingdoms. The Ancient of Days takes His throne, the books are opened, and “one like a son of man” comes with the clouds and receives an everlasting dominion. A boastful horn wars against the saints, but the kingdom is given to the saints of the Most High.
questions: How does Daniel 7 parallel Daniel 2?
Who is the “son of man” (7:13–14; Mark 14:62)?
What hope does 7:27 give God’s people?

chapterList.title: The Ram and the Goat
chapterList.summary: Daniel sees a ram with two horns (Media and Persia) trampled by a goat with one great horn (Greece). The horn breaks into four, and from one comes a little horn that exalts itself, attacks God’s people, and stops the sacrifices. Gabriel explains, and Daniel is overcome.
questions: How was this vision fulfilled in history (Alexander and his successors)?
What does the little horn reveal about proud rulers?
What assurance is given in 8:25?

chapterList.title: Daniel’s Prayer and the Seventy Weeks
chapterList.summary: Reading Jeremiah’s seventy years, Daniel prays, confessing Israel’s sin and pleading for mercy “not because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy.” Gabriel brings the vision of seventy weeks: to finish transgression, atone for iniquity, and bring everlasting righteousness. An anointed one will be cut off.
questions: How did Scripture prompt Daniel’s prayer (9:2)?
What is the basis of Daniel’s appeal (9:18–19)?
How is the Messiah’s work described in 9:24–26?

chapterList.title: The Heavenly Messenger
chapterList.summary: After three weeks of fasting, Daniel sees a glorious man by the Tigris. A messenger explains he was delayed 21 days by the prince of Persia until Michael helped him. He strengthens Daniel: “O man greatly loved, fear not, peace be with you.”
questions: What does this chapter reveal about spiritual warfare?
How does the heavenly messenger strengthen Daniel?
What does it mean to you that Daniel was “greatly loved”?

chapterList.title: Kings of the North and South
chapterList.summary: The messenger describes conflicts between Persia, Greece, and the kings of the north (Seleucids) and south (Ptolemies). A contemptible king (Antiochus IV) desecrates the temple and sets up the abomination of desolation, “but the people who know their God shall stand firm and take action.” The vision moves toward the end.
questions: What does the detailed history show about God’s knowledge of the future?
How do the faithful respond to persecution (11:32–35)?
How does Jesus refer to the abomination of desolation (Matthew 24:15)?

chapterList.title: The Time of the End
chapterList.summary: Michael will arise in a time of trouble, and God’s people will be delivered. “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame.” The wise will shine like stars. Daniel is told to seal the book and to go his way and rest, for he will rise to his reward.
questions: What does 12:2 teach about the resurrection?
How do the wise shine (12:3)?
What comfort is in God’s final words to Daniel (12:13)?

tagline: Faithful in exile under the Most High who rules the kingdoms of men
readingPlan: 12 chapters: one chapter a day takes 12 days; two a day takes about 6 days. For each chapter, read it on ESV.org, then come back here for the summary, questions, and your notes.
